assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 8,000 req/s at steady state, 90% browse / 7% book / 3% order lookup. This is the QUIET shape. The defining stress of a ticketing system is the flash sale, when traffic multiplies AND browsing collapses into buying — run that as a what-if against this baseline rather than reading the baseline as the worst case.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: One seat-inventory primary sized at ~3,000 writes/s — deliberately the lowest capacity in the design. A seat decrement takes a row lock, so inventory writes do not scale by adding app servers, and this is the component a flash sale actually breaks.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Booking writes are serialised through a queue so two buyers cannot take the same seat. The engine models the queue as a service centre with a rate; it does NOT model ordering, hold timers, or the oversell that a lost message would cause. Correctness of the reservation protocol is out of scope here.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Seat-availability reads are served from Redis with an assumed ~88% hit rate on browse (replica visit_prob 0.12). During a sale the availability map churns on every purchase, so this hit rate is optimistic exactly when it matters most.

assumptions.subject: pay
assumptions.statement: 'Payment service' is the tier YOU run: it holds the outbound connection to the PSP and waits ~150 ms per charge (~60 in-flight charges per instance). The PSP itself (Stripe/Adyen-class) is NOT modelled — Keystone has no per-instance price for a third-party API, and inventing one would be a fabricated number. In production the PSP's server-enforced rate limit is a HARD 429 ceiling, not the graceful slowdown this queueing model shows.

assumptions.subject: waiting_room
assumptions.statement: No virtual waiting room / queue-it front door is modelled. Every real high-demand ticketing system has one, and it is the mechanism that keeps the numbers in this model from being fiction on sale day.

assumptions.subject: app
assumptions.statement: App tier at ~2,000 req/s per instance across a mixed read/write handler set; 6 instances gives roughly 1.3x headroom to the 85% ceiling at this load.

_library.summary: Browse-heavy event pages in front of a row-locked seat inventory that a sale turns write-bound.
